preamble: Denasalization of the close-mid nasal vowel [ẽ] to oral [e]. In Latin, word-final -m and n before s were reduced to nasalization of the preceding vowel (decem [ˈdɛkẽː], mensem), and Vulgar Latin then lost that nasality, giving oral long vowels (mēse > Italian mese). In medieval Galician-Portuguese, loss of intervocalic /n/ left a nasal vowel in hiatus (Latin vēna > vẽa, plēnum > chẽo, tenēre > tẽer); when the following vowel was as open or more open, the nasality was lost, giving vea, cheo and teer (later Portuguese veia, cheio, ter).

examples.note: The nasal vowel left by loss of intervocalic /n/ denasalized before the more open /a/; Portuguese later inserted a glide.

examples.to: teer, then Galician and Portuguese ter
examples.note: After denasalization the two identical vowels contracted.

examples.from: Classical Latin mēnsem 'month', with n before s realized as nasalization of the vowel
examples.note: The vowels nasalized by lost n before s and by word-final m lost their nasality and merged with the oral long vowels.

examples.to: Italian dieci, with no trace of the nasal
examples.note: Word-final -m survived only as nasalization of the vowel, which was then lost without a trace in Romance.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). Latin phonology and orthography: Nasals. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_phonology_and_orthography
